procedural_history.originating_court: High Court of Judicature at Madras
procedural_history.impugned_order: Judgment and order of the High Court of Judicature at Madras dated 26th April, 2018 in Writ Petition No.19335 of 2017
procedural_history.high_court_proceedings: The High Court issued a writ of mandamus to transfer the investigation of a criminal case concerning the illegal manufacture and sale of Gutkha and Pan Masala, containing Tobacco and/or Nicotine, to the Central Bureau of Investigation (“CBI”). The High Court considered all aspects of the matter and was satisfied about the imperativeness of a fair investigation of the crime in question involving high ranking officials and the tentacles of the conspiracy in commission of the crime transcending beyond the State of Tamil Nadu and into different States.
procedural_history.supreme_court_posture: The petitioner, who was named as an accused in the FIR, filed a Special Leave Petition (Civil) No.13817 of 2018 challenging the High Court's order. The Supreme Court heard arguments from both sides and ultimately dismissed the special leave petition.

directions: The judgment under appeal is a nullity and liable to be set aside only on this score.

issue.issue_text: Whether the impugned judgment was liable to be set aside because the prayer for transfer of investigation to the CBI had already been considered and rejected by a Coordinate Bench of the same High Court in earlier writ petitions.

facts: A Coordinate Bench of the same High Court had previously heard a writ petition (W.P. No. 1846 of 2017) seeking to transfer the same investigation to the CBI.

In that earlier case, the Coordinate Bench rejected the transfer request, noting that the investigation by the state's Vigilance Commission was already "in progress" and that it was not necessary to transfer it at that time.
law: A court is not necessarily disregarding a binding precedent from a Coordinate Bench if it considers the prior decision and distinguishes the facts or circumstances of the current case from the earlier one.
application: The Supreme Court observed that the High Court, in the judgment under appeal, was fully aware of the earlier decision by the Coordinate Bench and had discussed it at length.
The Supreme Court found that the High Court had properly taken note of the earlier judgment and its reasoning.
The Court concluded that this was not a case of disregarding a binding precedent because the High Court had distinguished the earlier decision.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court rejected the petitioner's argument, holding that the High Court had not improperly disregarded the earlier decision. The Court found that the High Court was aware of the prior ruling, had duly considered it, and had distinguished it, which was a "possible view" and therefore not a valid ground to set aside the judgment.

issue.issue_text: Whether the impugned judgment is a nullity because the petitioner, though named as an accused in the FIR, was not given an opportunity of hearing nor was made a party in the public interest litigation.

facts: The petitioner was named as an accused in an FIR.
A public interest litigation (PIL) was filed, resulting in a judgment that transferred the investigation of the case to the CBI.
The petitioner was not made a party to this PIL and was not given an opportunity to be heard before the judgment was passed.
The petitioner argued that because he was not heard, the judgment was a nullity and should be set aside.
law: It is a well-settled legal principle that an accused person has no right to be heard at the stage of an investigation.
In a writ petition seeking an impartial investigation, the accused is not entitled to an opportunity of hearing as a matter of course.
An order passed behind a party's back may be a nullity if it results in a civil consequence for that party.
application: The Court applied the principle that an accused has no right to be heard during the investigation stage.
It reasoned that since the judgment in the PIL only entrusted the investigation to the CBI, it did not create a "civil consequence" for the petitioner that would require his participation.

The Court held that if an accused has no right to be heard during the investigation itself, they cannot argue that a direction to transfer that investigation to another agency is a nullity simply because they were not heard on the matter.
The Court concluded that the petitioner's absence as a party in the PIL was of "no avail" and could not be a basis to label the judgment a nullity.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court rejected the petitioner's argument, holding that the judgment was not a nullity. The Court reasoned that an accused has no right to be heard at the investigation stage, and therefore, the failure to make the petitioner a party or hear him before transferring the investigation to the CBI did not invalidate the judgment.

issue.issue_text: Whether the public interest litigation should have been dismissed on the ground that it was motivated by political vendetta.

facts: The petitioner argued that the public interest litigation (PIL) should be dismissed because it was politically motivated.
The PIL was filed by a member of the Legislative Assembly in Tamil Nadu (respondent No. 14).
law: The Court cited the legal principle from *K. Anbazhagan Vs. Superintendent of Police and Ors.*, which states that political opponents play an important role as "watchdogs of the Government in power."
According to this principle, political opponents can act as a "mouthpiece to ventilate the grievances of the public at large, if genuinely and unbiasedly projected."
application: The Court applied this principle by stating that a petition filed by a political figure cannot be automatically "brushed aside on the allegation of political vendetta."

The determining factor is not the motive of the person filing the petition, but whether the petition itself is genuine and raises a "reasonable apprehension of likelihood of bias in the dispensation of criminal justice system."
Since the Court found the petition to be genuine and raising valid concerns, the alleged political motivation of the filer was not a sufficient reason to dismiss it.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court concluded that this ground of challenge was "devoid of merits" and rejected the argument that the PIL should have been dismissed for being politically motivated.

ratio_decidendi.ratio: Ensuring a fair and impartial investigation against any person accused of the commission of a cognizable offence is imperative, with the primary emphasis on instilling faith in the public at large and the investigating agency.
obiter: Distinguishing a binding decision or precedent of a Coordinate Bench of the same High Court is not equivalent to disregarding it.

judicial_reasoning.core_finding: The High Court's judgment was a nullity and had to be set aside on the sole ground that the petitioner, who was named as an accused in the FIR, was not made a party to the public interest litigation nor given an opportunity to be heard. This procedural failure was dispositive of the appeal.
legal_tests_applied: A judgment is not considered to have disregarded a binding precedent from a Coordinate Bench if the subsequent judgment has distinguished the earlier decision.

A public interest litigation cannot be dismissed on the allegation of political vendetta if it is otherwise genuine and raises a reasonable apprehension of a likelihood of bias in the dispensation of the criminal justice system.
why_appellant_lost: The argument that the High Court disregarded a prior decision from a Coordinate Bench failed because the Supreme Court found that the High Court had, in fact, considered and distinguished the earlier judgment, which was a 'possible view' and therefore not a reversible error.

The argument that the public interest litigation was motivated by political vendetta was rejected because the court affirmed the principle that political opponents act as 'watchdogs of the Government in power' and their petitions should be considered on merit if they genuinely raise concerns about bias in the justice system.
why_respondent_won: The respondent prevailed on the issue of whether the High Court could order a CBI investigation despite a prior refusal by a Coordinate Bench, as the High Court had successfully distinguished the facts and context of the earlier cases.

The respondent succeeded in defending the legitimacy of the public interest litigation by establishing that the petitioner's status as a political opponent did not automatically disqualify the petition, which raised genuine concerns about the fairness of the state's investigation.
policy_considerations: The court underscored the imperativeness of ensuring a fair and impartial investigation to instill faith of the people in the fairness and impartiality of the investigation.

The court recognized the important role of political opponents as 'watchdogs of the Government in power' and as a 'mouthpiece to ventilate the grievances of the public at large,' suggesting that their participation in public interest litigation, when genuine, serves the public good.
